body_en:
Lately there's a line going around everywhere: sure, we have sixth-generation fighter jets, aircraft carriers, and all kinds of advanced gear — but we're still not safe. The spy cases uncovered recently are shocking. The short videos we scroll through on our phones every day are a battlefield where nations fight a war of public opinion. And some of our own people, without even realizing it, have picked the wrong side and handed a knife to the enemy.

Scare them first, then make the argument. The very first logical fallacy is already hiding in that opening.

1. Appeal to Fear: Scare Them First, and They Stop Thinking for Themselves

The claim:

Sure, we have sixth-generation fighter jets, aircraft carriers, and all kinds of advanced gear — but we're still not safe. The spy cases uncovered recently are shocking. The short videos we scroll through on our phones every day are a battlefield where nations fight a war of public opinion. And saddest of all, some of our own people, without even realizing it, have picked the wrong side and handed a knife to the enemy.

The rebuttal:

The fallacy here is the appeal to fear. The video opens with a show of force: first it tells you social media is a battlefield of public opinion, then it tells you some of your fellow citizens have already picked the wrong side and handed a knife to the enemy. Once the audience has swallowed the fear, their independent judgment is the first thing to go.

2. Three Fallacies in a Single Sentence: Straw Man, Equivocation, and Changing the Subject

The claim:

Just the other day, Canon closed its factory in Zhongshan, and the workers walked away with generous severance. The comments were full of praise: foreign companies have a conscience, they respect contracts, we should learn from them. Have you been drinking fake liquor or something? Foreign companies pay severance to their Chinese employees — is that because capitalists are kinder and more generous than we are?

The rebuttal:

There are three fallacies packed into this one attack.

The first is the straw man: twist your opponent's argument into something new, then attack the thing you invented so you can look like you won.

What the commenters actually said was that foreign companies “have a conscience and respect contracts” — and the heart of it is the contract part. Having a conscience is a subjective judgment; respecting contracts is a matter of fact. A quick aside: how do you tell a value judgment from a factual one? Check whether it can be proven wrong. You can't falsify “has a conscience” — it's a personal value judgment with no shared standard. But whether a company honored its contracts and labor law can be verified against contracts and arbitration records. That's a falsifiable fact.

The original argument was that “foreign companies in China pay severance by the book and honor their contracts.” That got twisted into “capitalists are kinder and more generous.” Nobody said that. It's a straw man the speaker built himself, then attacked furiously — swinging at an enemy that isn't there, fighting himself.

The second fallacy is equivocation. The sentence swaps “foreign companies” for “capitalists” — but capitalists exist everywhere, in every country. Then it swaps “Chinese employees” for “us” — and “us” covers a huge range of people, capitalists and employees alike. The definitions are blurred and stretched.

And once those concepts have been swapped, the original question — whether foreign companies pay severance by the book — has quietly become a nationalist showdown between “foreigners” and “us.” That's the third fallacy: changing the subject.

3. “Strict Laws Made Them Comply”? Single Cause and False Cause

The claim:

Do you have any idea how many policies and laws the government has put in place to protect Chinese employees working at foreign companies? Do you know how harshly labor inspectors come down on foreign companies that break the rules? Do you know that before a foreign company can send its profits out of China, it has to settle every debt — including employee severance — or its funds get frozen? Do you really think capitalists are that kind-hearted?

The rebuttal:

The fallacies here are the single-cause fallacy and false cause.

The logic runs: labor law is strict, so foreign companies are forced to comply. But there are many other reasons foreign companies follow labor law — compliance costs, brand and reputational risk, the risk of being sued, and the simple fact that multinationals follow local law as a matter of consensus. You can't pin it all on strict regulation.

Besides, labor law doesn't treat employees of foreign companies any differently from employees of private companies — and plenty of private firms face the same laws and still don't comply. So the inference “strict law, therefore companies are forced to comply” is a false cause.

4. The Microsoft Example: Believe It and You're Trapped; Fact-Check It and You're Trapped Too

The claim:

Open your eyes and look: in 2024, Microsoft shut down one of its companies in China and gave employees two choices. Stay in China and take severance of at least N+8. Go to the U.S. and work in Seattle. Those who stayed got generous payouts. Those who went to Seattle were laid off en masse a few months later, with not a cent of compensation. That's because 49 American states follow at-will employment: a company can fire you at any time, for any reason — or no reason at all — and owes you nothing. That's what their law says. So the engineers who stayed in China walked away with fat severance packages, while the ones who went to America had to borrow money for their plane tickets home.

The rebuttal:

Two kinds of people will hear this story. One group believes it unconditionally; the other rushes off to check whether it's true. Both fall into a trap.

The first group falls for cherry-picked evidence. The second falls for a changed subject. The original question was whether foreign companies in China pay severance by the book and honor their contracts. But this story has quietly swapped the question for a different one: how do foreign companies handle layoffs under their own country's laws? Those are two completely different questions.

So there's no need to argue over whether the story is true. Just go back to the original question. As the saying goes, a rumor takes one mouth to start and a hundred legs to chase down.

5. Appeal to Authority: What Can One Kissinger Quote Prove?

The claim:

Funny how these people never sing the praises of foreign companies. Former U.S. Secretary of State Henry Kissinger once said something worth pondering: “The Chinese have always been lucky — they always take good care of the bravest among them.”

The rebuttal:

The fallacy here is the appeal to authority. One sentence from Kissinger proves nothing. It's his personal feeling — or at most a piece of diplomatic flattery.

Who are these “bravest people”? The conspirators you keep talking about? The foreign bosses who honor their contracts? If they're so principled, why don't they honor contracts in Africa? Why do they strike in South America without even bothering to find a pretext? Why do they suddenly behave so well once they're in China?

Go look up the layoffs at Samsung China in 2019, Walmart in 2020, Dell in 2021, Apple in 2022, and Tesla Shanghai in 2023 — and ask who was actually protecting those workers. Someone is bravely protecting you, and all you can do is sing the praises of your foreign masters. What a shameless, sorry sight that is.

6. False Dichotomy: Praise a Foreign Company and You're a Traitor; Praise Regulation and You're a Patriot?

The claim:

Say that foreign companies in China pay severance by the book and honor their contracts, and you're singing the praises of foreigners — handing a knife to the enemy. Praise regulation, and you're a patriot.

The rebuttal:

The final fallacy is the false dichotomy. This either-or was deliberately manufactured after the concepts had already been swapped. Black-and-white thinking loves to take an open question and force it into two camps.

But the question could just as well be about how foreign companies and private companies compare when it comes to following labor law — or about acknowledging both that foreign companies comply with Chinese law and that Chinese regulation works. It's not one or the other.

Conclusion

Logic matters for every one of us. Without it, it's all too easy for a clever debater to dress up a nationalist showdown and swap out the question you were actually supposed to be asking.
excerpt_en: From a fear-mongering opening to Canon's factory closure and Microsoft's 2024 layoffs, this piece dismantles six fallacies one by one — straw men, false causes, appeals to authority, and a false choice between praising foreign firms and loving your country.
title_en: Logic Check: Is Praising a Foreign Company for Following the Rules “Handing a Knife to the Enemy”?
